hypothesis: The BF16 dot product has no ARM SIMD path upstream (AVX512/AVX2/SSE only), so it runs scalar on this device and dominates dense matmul time.
change: Added a hand-written NEON path (vshll + hardware vbfdotq_f32) for the BF16 dot product in the arch/arm ggml-cpu quant kernels.
action: Add NEON vshll + vbfdotq_f32 BF16 dot-product path
note: Configuration-sweep step 1.6 -> 2.3 t/s is +44%; the headline mirrored A/B quote is +40% decode / +55% prefill, with BF16 matmul time in the profile down 85%. The single largest decode win in the project.

hypothesis: Unpinned workers migrate across the two clusters, and this SoC has no L3, so every graph node pays a cross-cluster coherency round trip.
change: Added the stock flag pair --cpu-mask 0x3f --cpu-strict 1 so all six main-pool workers stay inside the 6-core perf-cluster cache domain.
action: Pin decode threads to the 6-core cluster (--cpu-mask 0x3f --cpu-strict 1)
note: +26% decode (3.5 -> 4.4 t/s), quality-neutral, still part of the shipping flag set.

hypothesis: The stock expert reduction builds 10 views plus 9 adds per layer, bloating the decode graph without doing arithmetic the model needs.
change: Added GGML_OP_MOE_SUM, a single-pass expert reduction replacing the 9-add chain.
action: Add GGML_OP_MOE_SUM single-pass expert reduction
note: ADD nodes per token fell 584 -> 152 (~-30% of the graph) with bit-identical output. Decode is unchanged (3.1 vs 3.1-3.2 t/s): this is a size/clarity win, not a speed lever.

hypothesis: With one token, the stock mul_mat_id walk has every thread steal 16-row chunks inside the same expert, so all threads miss the same TLB entries and fault together.
change: Flattened expert work into contiguous whole-expert units claimed from a single counter; shipped default ON at commit 9058ea6, env switch BONSAI_MULMATID_FLAT.
action: Default-on BONSAI_MULMATID_FLAT flat expert work distribution
note: +4.8% decode, bit-identical, and major faults collapsed 719 -> 318 per token. The fault reduction came with less work, which is why it converted into speed where the later WILLNEED shield did not.

hypothesis: A 2.8 GB MTP sidecar could draft tokens cheaply enough to beat single-token decode even at only ~1.8 tokens per pass.
change: Enabled MTP speculative decoding (draft-n-max 1) with the 2.8 GB MTP head loaded alongside the model.
action: Enable MTP speculative decoding
note: 4x slower (3.94 -> 0.95 t/s) despite 77.5% acceptance: the sidecar evicts the expert working set and major faults rise 1,130 -> 6,100 per token. Closed. Revisit only if the sidecar can be shrunk below the page-cache cliff (~2.79 GB -> ~1 GB by requantising blk.48 experts to Q2_0).

hypothesis: A small static set of frequently routed experts could be pinned in cache for a large hit-rate gain.
change: Analysed per-expert routing frequency across the corpus to pick a static hot set.
action: Assess static hot-expert pinning
note: Modern fine-grained MoEs are load-balanced (near-uniform global expert frequency), so a static pin captures only ~45% of routed slots and starves the dynamic tail. Closed without a device block.

numbers.cause: load-balanced routing; starves the dynamic tail

hypothesis: MADV_HUGEPAGE on the read-only weight mapping would give the expert path 2 MB pages and multiply TLB reach.
change: Added BONSAI_THP in llama-mmap.cpp to hint MADV_HUGEPAGE on the mmap weight mapping; measured mirrored off/on/on/off.
action: Hint MADV_HUGEPAGE on the file-backed weight mapping
note: Inert for translation (FilePmdMapped stayed 0 kB; f2fs on 6.6 never calls mapping_set_large_folios()) and harmful via reclaim: Rss fell 17.3 -> 9.0 GB as the hint evicted the expert working set, and decode fell ~45%. Only uncommitted change left in the tree.

hypothesis: The 1.52x single-threaded speedup from a second accumulator in the Q2_0 kernel would show up end to end.
change: Measured tools/q2_0_bench.c with BONSAI_Q20_UNROLL=0/1, then ran the engine at unpinned -t 2 and pinned -t 6.
action: Measure Q2_0 dual-accumulator unroll end to end
note: 1.52x in the microbenchmark (6.2 -> 9.4 Mrow/s) but zero end-to-end change at two thread counts: at 2+ threads another worker's chain already hides the latency the unroll targets, and the expert path is not purely ALU-bound. Kernel micro-optimisation is closed as a lever; the unroll itself is kept as the default.

hypothesis: mul_mat_id serialises on ~1,440 barriers per token, so barrier removal is a large lever.
change: Read ggml-cpu.c:1640-1841 and counted the synchronisation points.
action: Audit the 1,440-barriers-per-token claim
note: Claim is false: the function has exactly ONE ggml_barrier, at ggml-cpu.c:1771 before the per-expert loop, and upstream already uses a per-expert atomic counter. Closed as a misinformation trap that cost real time.

hypothesis: Stock dense mul_mat work-stealing makes threads jump between 64-row chunks; giving each thread one contiguous slice plus a row-group prefetch should cut dense time.
change: Implemented BONSAI_MULMAT_FLAT (default OFF) in ggml-cpu.c: contiguous ne01 slices for ne11==ne12==ne13==1 && ne01>=64, prefetch every 8 rows; added BONSAI_MULMAT_FLAT_REPORT to prove the path ran.
action: Implement flat static partitioning for the dense single-token mul_mat
note: Neutral: token-identical (md5 20e5b49647ecfe3cfcf354b9e15ce587 across all ten runs) and the path is live (~420 dense mul_mat calls/token), but 4 mirrored pairs gave +1.45/-4.06/+1.20/+8.62% and the +1.67% point estimate (t=0.69) sits inside the noise floor. Majflt unchanged, so no mechanism signature. Ships opt-in OFF at commit 10288ca.

hypothesis: A matching scaling_max_freq cap profile means two arms are comparable.
change: Repeated an identical arm in a later block and compared decode at an identical cap profile before and after the arm.
action: Quantify the arm-to-arm noise floor
note: Methodology correction that governs every later decision: repeating the SAME arm moved decode by up to 7.9% (a2: 4.7977 then 4.4450) with an identical cap profile, so a matching profile is necessary but not sufficient. A 4-arm mirrored block cannot resolve the few-percent effects this project hunts; ~16 pairs are needed for 2%. Prefer harnesses that remove variance over averaging it.

numbers.example: a2 4.7977 then 4.4450 at identical cap profile

hypothesis: The two prime cores are idle under 0x3f; adding them with -t 8 --cpu-mask 0xff should raise decode.

note: 14-18% SLOWER than 0x3f (4.107/3.958 vs 4.6027-4.7977, gate re-check 4.8024). Placement is not the failure: field 39 shows the eight workers placed 1:1 across cpu0-7, 100% sticky, no bunching. The workload is memory-bound, so the prime cluster adds core clock and cross-cluster barriers, not bandwidth. 0xff is closed as a lever.

hypothesis: A targeted Python GGUF writer can requantise selected dense tensors without touching the expert pool.

change: Built varH with llama-quantize --allow-requantize --keep-split --tensor-type 'hc_.*_(up|down)\.weight$=q8_0' COPY 16; shard 2 came out byte-identical; gated on host with 32-chunk paired wikitext-2 PPL.

DISCREPANCY CARRIED FORWARD: this stage records +0.092% (t=1.02, 26/32 chunks worse) while the corrected per-chunk method in Stage 5 computes +0.290% overall / +0.300% paired (t=1.18) against a re-run baseline - Stage 5 flags it as unresolved. hypothesis: varH plus output.weight Q4_0 together (the full rewrite) maximise the dense byte saving.
change: Converted both families in one llama-quantize COPY run (638.3 MiB saved) and gated on host with 32-chunk paired PPL, after an 8-chunk run read only +0.408%.

hypothesis: The full rewrite's 638.3 MiB byte saving should show up as a decode (and some prefill) win on device.
change: Staged both models on /sdcard and ran two mirrored A/B/B/A decode blocks plus a redesigned 256-token prefill block with mqdense_arm.sh/mqdense_run.sh.
action: Measure the full rewrite on device (decode + prefill)
note: Decode: group means shipping 4.798 vs q8dense 4.933 = +2.82% (per-block +3.06/+2.55), best fully cap-stable pair +6.30%, one negative pair -1.08%, 3/4 positive - a direction, not a proven effect at the 5-8% noise floor. Prefill: +1.24% group means (6.4313 -> 6.5110), inside the noise. Superseded: varH alone later measured +8.19% decode (iteration 22), so the expensive part (output.weight) was negative on speed as well as quality. The 966-token prefill block was unusable - all four arms throttled mid-arm; a 256-token prompt fixed it.

hypothesis: A model copy staged under /data/local/tmp is equivalent to one on /sdcard because stat -f shows the same f2fs filesystem.
change: Pushed the rewritten pair to /data/local/tmp/mf-model/ and ran the identical harness; then copied the same bytes to /sdcard and re-ran.
action: Stage the model on /data/local/tmp
note: 0.09 t/s (11 s/token) vs 4.76 t/s for the SAME sha256-verified bytes on /sdcard, with read_bytes climbing at 2.9 GB/s to 1.9 TB and never converging. dd reads the pushed copy sequentially at 2.8 GB/s, so it is the physical layout of the adb-push copy in a nearly-full f2fs volume (~50x slower on the ~460 KB random expert slices). Rule adopted: models always staged on /sdcard, and validate every new copy with one decode arm first.

hypothesis: -tb 8 makes the prefill threadpool inherit --cpu-mask 0x3f, so prefill already runs pinned on the 6-core cluster.
change: Traced postprocess_cpu_params (common/common.cpp:294-301) and confirmed on device; added --cpu-mask-batch 0xff --cpu-strict-batch 1 and ran two mirrored 256-token prefill blocks (TB2/TB3).
action: Pin the batch (prefill) threadpool 1:1 across all 8 cores
note: The shipping flags were wrong by accident: -tb 8 sets cpuparams_batch.n_threads=8, which makes postprocess_cpu_params SKIP the cpu-params copy, leaving an all-zero cpumask and NO affinity at all (19 of 24 threads carried Cpus_allowed_list 0-7). Explicit pinning is worth +21.5% prefill (groups 7.4650 -> 9.0716, pairs +23.69/+21.78/+15.03/+26.16, t=9.08, df 3, 4/4 positive, distributions non-overlapping). The largest single result in Stage 3 and flag-only - no engine patch.

numbers.placement: 19 of 24 threads unpinned before; 14 pinned to cpu0-5, 0 ggml workers on cpu6/7 after

hypothesis: The +21.5% prefill win could be an artefact of measuring prefill alone, or could heat the device enough to hurt a following decode.
change: Ran block TB4: one streamed request with a 256-token prefill plus 64 decode tokens, A = unpinned, B = pinned 0xff, mirrored A/B/B/A.
action: Validate batch pinning in a realistic prefill+decode request
note: The win survives and decode does not regress: prefill +17.94% group mean (pairs +21.02/+14.93), decode +3.46% group mean (pairs +2.69/+4.23), 4/4 positive. The decode delta is inside the 5-8% spread, so treat it as neutral-to-mildly-positive, not a second effect - the point is the change is safe end-to-end. This is the arm that justifies adding the flag to shipping.

hypothesis: If 8 unpinned prefill threads beat 6 threads, confining prefill to the 6-core cluster (-tb 6 pinned 0x3f) should be worse than unpinned but better than nothing.
change: Ran block TB1: A = -tb 8 unpinned, B = -tb 6 with --cpu-mask-batch 0x3f --cpu-strict-batch 1, mirrored 256-token prefill.
action: Confine prefill to the 6-core cluster (-tb 6 pinned 0x3f)
note: Neutral: +1.38% group mean, pairs -1.32/+4.30 (sign disagreement), t=0.53 (df 1). Prefill is compute-bound, so the two prime cores earn their keep there, unlike decode where 0xff measured 14-18% slower. Closed; the winning configuration is -tb 8 pinned to 0xff, not -tb 6. This block doubles as the position control that proves the +21.5% belongs to the flag (2nd/3rd slots ran +1.38% here vs +21.5% in TB2/TB3).

hypothesis: varH's host PPL passes and its dense byte saving should show up as a device decode win on its own, without the rejected output.weight conversion.
change: Staged varH on /sdcard with sha256 verification, ran one throwaway warmup arm (5.6199 t/s) to prove the copy was not fragmented, then two mirrored A/B/B/A decode blocks (64 tokens) with a 5 s cap sampler per arm.
action: Measure varH alone on device (decode)
note: +8.19% decode group mean (shipping 5.1883 vs varH 5.6135), pairs +7.37/+10.86/+5.49/+9.22 = mean +8.23%, sd 2.32, SE 1.16, t=7.09 (df 3), 4/4 positive, all eight arms cap-stable at 3532800/3840000 with no sample falling to 2841600. The first dense result that clears the Stage 1 noise floor on its own terms. majflt is also lower on varH (13,857-16,340 vs 15,547-17,099 per 64 tokens). This is the arm that ships varH.

hypothesis: The post-prefill decode dip (first 16 tokens at ~77% of steady state) is caused by page faults, so POSIX_MADV_WILLNEED on the dense tensors at the transition should shorten it.
change: Added BONSAI_SHIELD option A in llama-context.cpp (WILLNEED the 1079 dense tensors once, excluding the 26.8 GiB PLE table) and ran mirrored A/B/B/A (shield 0 vs 1), 256-token prefill + 64 decode in one request.
action: Shield post-prefill decode with MADV_WILLNEED on dense tensors
note: Mechanism confirmed, no speedup: decode-phase major faults fall 70-79% (e.g. 14,668 -> 3,096/s) and total majflt -36.9%, but decode is +0.33% (n.s.), early-decode +1.8%, steady-state -0.3%. The dip is I/O-volume-bound, not fault-bound: the same bytes still come off storage, only the accounting changes. Token identity holds (md5 f1ac9c8a77541e447f1f4810a8cadc73, 170 B) across shield 0/1/2. Stays in the tree env-gated, default off.

hypothesis: Turning off fault-around and readahead on the expert tensors during prefill (MADV_RANDOM) stops prefill from pulling in unrouted neighbour pages and reduces eviction.
change: Added BONSAI_SHIELD option B in llama-context.cpp (MADV_RANDOM the 144 expert tensors during prefill, back to NORMAL at the first decode ubatch) and ran mirrored A/B/B/A (shield 0 vs 2).
action: Shield prefill with MADV_RANDOM on expert tensors
note: Falsified and a dead end: prefill -32.68% (7.4133 -> 4.9907), decode -8.99%, major faults +648.8% (287,357 -> 2,151,790, i.e. 2.87e5 -> 2.15e6). Disabling fault-around converts the kernel's amortised bulk reads into ~7.5x as many individual faults. The readahead on this access pattern is useful work, not waste. Mode 3 (both) is dominated by this harm and was not given a block.

hypothesis: The decode budget can be attributed per op, per weight type and per fault, so the next lever can be chosen from measurement instead of guesswork.
change: Extended BONSAI_PROF with per-weight tracking keyed on src[0] (time, calls, bytes) and per-graph page-fault counters (weight table raised from 1024 to 4096 entries after the LM head was silently dropped); differenced BONSAI_PROF_EVERY=1 dumps over the last 48 graphs of a 98-graph run, three decode arms and one prefill arm.
action: Build the per-op / per-type decode and prefill budget
note: Decode is 173.229 ms/token = 5.773 t/s of pure compute against 5.610-5.788 measured, reconciling end to end with no unattributed gap. The two matmuls are 86.8% of decode. A major fault costs ~170 us (two independent regressions: 166.5/168.2 us) and the correlation lives ENTIRELY in the expert path (dense r=-0.04/-0.15). Of the expert path's 62.49 ms/token excess over the dense rate for the same bytes, 19.6 ms (31%) is fault stalls and the residual 42.9 ms is the Q2_0 compute path itself. Prefill: 113.976 ms/token = 8.77 t/s compute vs 8.574 measured, MUL_MAT_ID 61.9%.

hypothesis: Copying the 1079 dense tensors into an anonymous buffer backed by 2 MB pages would make the dense backbone immune to page-cache eviction during prefill.
change: Built /data/local/tmp/thp_probe (MoeDroid/tools/thp_probe.c) to map anonymous memory, hint MADV_HUGEPAGE, touch every page, then attempt MADV_COLLAPSE (25) and report AnonHugePages at each step.
action: Probe anonymous THP feasibility for the dense weights
note: Hard ceiling of ~207-210 huge pages (~420 MiB) regardless of mapping size: 14.0% coverage at 2908 MiB, 14.4% aligned, 5.1% at 8192 MiB - going from 2.9 GB to 8 GB bought zero extra huge pages (210 -> 209). MADV_COLLAPSE returns ENOMEM past the ceiling; defrag=[never] and not writable without root, so nothing compacts and only order-9 blocks already free in the buddy allocator are usable. Alignment is not the limit. The anonymous dense-cache plan would get 14% PMD coverage and pay a copy for nothing; an 8 GB anonymous expert cache would get 5% and take RAM from the page cache that gives the 99.8% expert hit rate. Closed.

hypothesis: Prefill throughput varies monotonically with the physical microbatch -ub, so a smaller value trades memory for speed predictably.
change: Ran a 518-token prefill sweep over -ub 512/256/128/64 in descending and ascending order, then a mirrored A/B/B/A (64/256/256/64) at matched temperature, with a 90 s cooldown and the cap gate before every arm.
action: Sweep the physical microbatch (-ub) for prefill
note: Non-monotonic and the middle values are traps: means 512 = 10.6525, 64 = 10.2795, 256 = 9.0717, 128 = 8.9656 t/s (~19% spread). The one fully cap-stable pair at matched temperature (start 91.5 vs 93.0 C) gives -14.85% for -ub 256 vs -ub 64; group means are -11.8%. Slot position was confounded with the value in both ordered passes (slots 1&4 always held {512,64}, 2&3 held {256,128}); the mirror pass broke it. Keep the default 512. Do NOT quote the prefill/decode major-fault split as a -ub signal (22x swing on history). Closed for 256/128; the non-monotonic shape needs a randomised design, not an explanation.

hypothesis: ik_llama.cpp may be substantially faster on this device and could serve as a measured oracle for the remaining headroom.
change: Cloned ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp @ 8313388a, cross-compiled for Android arm64 with the same NDK flags plus -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON -DGGML_IQK_MUL_MAT=ON, pushed libomp.so, loaded our varH UNMODIFIED, and ran matched flags with q8_0 KV on both sides (best vs best).

hypothesis: Stages 3/4 and the Stage 5 oracle run are directly comparable because the model, flags and cap profile are the same.

hypothesis: The dense q3_K + q2_0 tensors are unpack-bound, so requantising them to q4_K should convert Stage 4's measured headroom into decode speed.
change: Parsed the varH inventory and built varD4 with an explicit anchored 148-name override list (90 q3_K + 58 q2_0, 545.89 MiB; token_embd.weight and all 144 experts excluded) via llama-quantize --allow-requantize --keep-split --tensor-type-file COPY 16, then gated on host with 32-chunk paired PPL.
action: Requantise dense q3_K + q2_0 to q4_K (varD4)
note: FAILS the quality gate: +0.613% paired PPL (t=2.01, SE 0.313) for a predicted +5.8% decode. Mechanism: the round-trip is q3_K -> F32 -> q4_K, and the F32 values are the already-lossy q3_K reconstruction, so the target adds a second quantization on top of the first - converting to a higher bit width can still lose quality. Rejected on quality, device decode never run.

hypothesis: q8_0 is the safe fallback for the dense outliers because it is the fastest dense type per byte (50.0 GiB/s).
change: Built varD8 (same 148 anchored names -> q8_0), verified shard 2 byte-identical, staged on /sdcard with a warmup arm (sha256 matched host), then ran two mirrored A/B/B/A decode blocks against varH.
action: Requantise dense q3_K + q2_0 to q8_0 (varD8)
note: Passes PPL (+0.107%, t=0.50) but is measurably SLOWER: group means varH 5.5294 vs varD8 5.3143 = -3.89%, pairs -4.12/-6.32/-3.29/-1.74 = mean -3.87%, sd 1.91, 4/4 negative. Rate is only half the trade - q8_0 is 2.5x the bytes of q3_K, so per token it is the slowest of the three candidates because it inflates the smallest-byte tensors the most. Rejected on measurement, not just arithmetic. (Note: STAGE5-report.md:17 says -4 to -6%; its own 2.3 measures -3.87%/-3.89%, which is what is recorded here.)

hypothesis: q5_K is the last point where the dense rate gain still beats the byte cost, so varD5 should pass quality AND win ~3.2% decode.
change: Built varD5 (same 148 anchored names -> q5_K), staged on /sdcard with a warmup arm (5.8196 t/s), then ran FOUR mirrored A/B/B/A decode blocks (8 pairs) against varH, all arms cap-stable.
action: Requantise dense q3_K + q2_0 to q5_K (varD5)
note: The only varD variant that wins on both axes, but the win is small and not formally significant: PPL -0.117% (t=-0.43, marginally BETTER than varH) and decode +1.95% pairs mean over 8 pairs (group means 5.5874 -> 5.6923 = +1.88%), sd 3.35, SE 1.19, t=1.64 (df 7), 7/8 positive, 95% CI -0.86% to +4.75%. The observed mean sits 1.6 SE below the +3.2% prediction, so the true effect is more likely small than large. action: Run P3a Gate 3(b) for MOE_X4=2 on device, then test whether its failure clause discriminates

The controls settle what the drift clause means: an identical-config rerun is BIT-REPRODUCIBLE (max drift 0.000e+00 over 8 chunks), so the churn is the flag's, not noise; and at the real shapes the kernel is as accurate as stock (mode2 1.144e-5 at nb=40 vs reference-vs-oracle 9.797e-6; 3.815e-6 at nb=10 vs 3.952e-6), so it is not a kernel defect. Equally-accurate-but-differently-associated kernels flip near-tie tokens, which moves a chunk's g_i by ~1e-2 while the paired mean stays at zero - so the point-wise 5e-3 bound is ZERO for the identical-code null and ~1e-2 for every true alternative, i.e. it cannot discriminate and no genuine kernel change can pass it.
